value.overview: Lesson’s Seedeater is a small finch-like tanager of open, grassy habitats in northern South America. It is best known for its seasonal movements between breeding areas in the Guianas, Venezuela, Colombia, and Trinidad and Tobago and nonbreeding areas farther west and south in the Amazon Basin. The species is an unusual visitor in Central America. In Costa Rica, it is considered a very rare vagrant rather than a regular resident or migrant.
value.classification: Lesson’s Seedeater belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the seedeater genus Sporophila. Its scientific name is Sporophila bouvronides.
value.identification: This small, short-tailed seedeater has a thick, conical bill. The adult male is chiefly black above and on the head, with prominent white markings on the face and underparts, including a strong white moustache or whisker stripe. The female is much duller, with olive-brown upperparts, pale yellowish or buff underparts, and a dull yellowish bill. Females and immature birds can be difficult to distinguish from similar Sporophila species without close views or an accompanying male.
value.rangeHabitat: Lesson’s Seedeater breeds from northern Colombia and Venezuela east through Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, and Trinidad and Tobago. During the nonbreeding season it moves into parts of western Amazonia, including eastern Peru, western Brazil, and northern Bolivia. It uses shrubby savannas, tall grasslands, forest edges, cultivated areas, second growth, and open wetlands or riverine habitats, often near water. In Costa Rica, the species is known from a documented vagrant record at Tortuguero, Limón Province, on 25 June 2022, in the country’s northeastern lowlands.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance seasonal migrant in South America. Costa Rica is outside its regular range; the Tortuguero observation represents vagrancy, possibly associated with weather systems over the Caribbean and northern South America, rather than an established migration route.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in the northern part of the species’ South American range, including the Guianas, northern Venezuela and Colombia, and Trinidad and Tobago. Like other Sporophola seedeaters, it is believed to build a small cup-shaped nest in shrubs or low vegetation and to raise its young in open habitats with abundant grasses. Detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care is limited. There is no evidence that Lesson’s Seedeater breeds regularly in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists chiefly of grass and other small seeds, taken from seed heads or picked from the ground. It may also consume a limited amount of other plant material and possibly small invertebrates, especially when feeding young. Individuals often forage in grassy clearings, marshy open areas, river islands, agricultural margins, and scrub. The species may occur in small groups or mixed flocks with other seedeaters when food is concentrated.
value.behavior: Lesson’s Seedeater is an active, inconspicuous bird of dense grass and low scrub. It commonly moves through vegetation while searching for seeds and may perch briefly on exposed stems or shrubs. Males are more readily detected because of their contrasting black-and-white plumage and calls. Seasonal movements can cover long distances, and the species is capable of appearing well outside its normal range. In Costa Rica, observers should document plumage, vocalizations, photographs, and habitat carefully because confusion with other seedeaters is possible.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliable evidence indicates a major global population decline, although detailed population information is limited.
